utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljkovic, before we move forward, I'd like to just clear up something from yesterday, and it's having to do with the tape recording that you made of the threats against you. My question to you is: After you made the tape recording of the conversation and General Boskovic made a transcript of the recording, did Frenki Simatovic come and ask you for the tapes? Did he ask you to give him the tapes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did come and ask me to give him the tapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can have a minute. The headset seems to be out of order.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And after he requested the tapes, you had a meeting with Mr. Stanisic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, I was at Frenki's, at his home, when Stanisic entered. He shook hands with me and he said, "I'm glad to see that you're still good friends after everything that has happened, and I hope we will be able to bury our axes and overcome everything that has happened," and that is where it ended. I never gave him the tapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. I want to now ask that the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 389, tab 8. I'm going to ask that the witness actually be handed the original. I'd ask you to take a look at this document, Mr. Vasiljkovic, and I'd ask you, after you arrived here at The Hague, were you given an opportunity to look at and read this document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And is it a report in order signed by General Tolimir of the 1st Krajina Corps, the 28th of July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The Chamber will be able to read the entirety of this document, but would it be fair to say this is a rather lengthy report by General Tolimir regarding his assessment of volunteers and paramilitaries in the Bosnian theatre?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is a document in which he presents his views about volunteers, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that his views are generally quite negative regarding the role of volunteers in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think it would be correct to say that they were extremely negative and that, through this report, he expresses his own great mistrust towards volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention to a particular portion of the report, and it will be displayed on the television screen in front of you, but again you have the original if the glare from the lights makes it hard to read. I'm going to ask you to just read this particular paragraph that's been enlarged on the screen in front of you now. Are you able to see that with the lights?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could you please read that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In the area of the Serbian municipality of Skelani, a camp of so-called Red Berets was established, headed by Nikola Pupovac, one of Captain Dragan's pupils. According to unconfirmed reports, this group is preparing to overthrow the government and take power in the Serbian municipality of Skelani."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you recognise the name Nikola Pupovac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I think he was one of my students in Golubic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you have any personal knowledge regarding this so-called camp of Red Berets established in Skelani?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge about this because here too it says "unconfirmed reports."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm now going to direct your attention to another portion of this report. It's going to be highlighted now in a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could give me the page number in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just a second, Your Honour. It's page 9, Your Honour, and it's the second paragraph at the top of that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljkovic, could I please ask you to read this paragraph from the report.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "A so-called special company has been formed in the territory of the municipality of Teslic. It is formally a part of the Teslic Serbian Brigade but it is in fact under the influence of individuals from the municipal structures in the municipality of Teslic. This company has about 80 members, mostly criminals, under the command of Dracen Jocic. A platoon of the so-called Serbian Guards has also joined this company. Members of this company completed a nine-day training course organised by the Red Berets from Mount Ozren. This company carries out 'special tasks' on the defence line without informing the brigade command."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you have any personal knowledge of a nine-day training course organised by the Red Berets from Mount Ozren?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not even be able to point to Ozren on the map. I was never there, nor was I ever in Teslic, so I simply don't know why you're linking this to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, I'm not linking it to you, sir, I'm just asking whether you have any knowledge or information you can contribute regarding it. How about the name of Dracen Jocic? Do you recognise that name?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The name doesn't mean anything to me. I think it's in Republika Srpska. I wasn't there, so I don't know why ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The last couple of sentences I'd ask you to look at from this report -- and for the Chamber, that -- on the English translation, it's page 10, it's the second paragraph from the bottom. Mr. Vasiljkovic, could I ask you to read that portion there.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Krajina special police with 45 men led by Zivojin Ivanovic, also known as Crnogorac, is present in the area of Brcko. He has not placed himself under the command of the Brcko Brigade. He was allegedly sent by the Serbian SUP."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you recognise the name Zivojin Ivanovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know it very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is that the same Ivanovic that you spoke about yesterday?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume it could be the same one. As I wasn't there, I can't be sure, but name is the same as the Ivanovic that I mentioned, and I have reason to believe that it was him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 389, tab 9. And that will also be displayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We're handing you a hard copy of that. It will also be displayed on the monitor in front of you. I'd ask you to take a look at the name and signature of this document dated the 9th of July, 1992. Do you recognise that signature?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think it is Zika Ivanovic, Crnogorac.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, can you read for us the heading, the listing of where this particular document is originating from, the upper left-hand corner of the document.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: SAO, the Serbian Autonomous Region of Semberija and Majevica, unit for special purposes Brcko, date July 9, 1992. I think this was during the breakthrough of the corridor when many men participated in this operation of the breakthrough of the corridor. At least, that is what I assume it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Chamber, if you know, the significance of special purposes unit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid you have to be more specific. You mean generally or this particular unit that you're speaking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Generally.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you how I think it was generally speaking in Yugoslavia. After the battle for Glina, the Knindza, who were then the special forces of the Krajina police, gained a significant reputation so that almost all those who fought there consider themselves to be special units or Knindza or Red Berets, so that my understanding of a special unit differs drastically from the special units that I saw on the ground. As far as this particular unit is concerned, I think it was specially formed of volunteers who had come from all over when the corridor was being stormed to the Republic of Srpska Krajina. So I don't think that Zika Ivanovic was in Brcko all the time. He was in this operation in which the whole of the Krajina took part, and men from Republika Srpska. I think there were a lot of reports about this, and I am informed about it solely from -- by the press.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that it was common for a -- it was common for many different units to take on the title or incorporate into the title of their unit "special purposes unit"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. I think that there were more special purpose units than regular units. I rarely came across someone who said, "I was just a soldier." Everyone over there was a so-called "specialjalist" or a member of a special unit. It didn't mean much to me. It just meant that he was a fighter down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to proceed in the questioning a little bit out of order. If I could direct your attention to paragraph Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 71 of the witness summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljkovic, I'd ask you now -- you've mentioned earlier regarding how, during the summer of 1991, you had the idea for the formation of the Captain Dragan Fund. Could I ask you to describe in a little greater detail what the fund was and what was the goal of the fund.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I was replaced, or once I had realised that I would have no more opportunity to fight in the armed forces of my country, as I mentioned yesterday, there was an aura of popularity around me, and I wanted to use that popularity for something good. I didn't wish to get involved in politics in those days, and it occurred to me, as I visited some hospitals and seeing the wounded arriving there were not taken care of properly because Serbia was not officially at war, so there was no law to take care of the wounded. So I decided to use the media popularity I had to set up a fund that would care for the victims of war. The fund was formed with the aim of assisting all the physical victims of the war. More than 67.000 people have received aid from the foundation, of which 14.000 were children, of which 1.500 were born after their fathers were killed. So it's a wonderful institution which had more than 300.000 donors, and I think that all the bodies, including the authorities and individuals, assisted this institution and it has grown into a very large institution which has 12 years of work behind it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you this: Can you briefly describe what would be the process if a former soldier who was, let's say, permanently disabled in the war, what would be the basic process for that soldier to make a claim and receive assistance from the fund?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the work of the fund was public from the very first day, and this is stated in the statute. So anyone who wishes to look at our documents is free to do so. Secondly, a combatant or a representative of his or, rather, the victim of the war should come, or his representative, to fill in certain forms to provide some evidence that he was wounded and to fill in this form indicating which unit he was a member of, when this happened, a brief description of his wounding, or killing if it's a relative, upon which he would be given aid depending on the category that the combatant would be ranked within.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Once a person fills out the paperwork saying where they were injured and how they were injured, did the fund take any steps to verify the accuracy of that information?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fund did have access to almost all the institutions in the country. Yes, we had a large team of people doing this, and whenever we felt it necessary, we would check the information given to us. I don't know whether this was done in each and every case when it was obvious that the documents were correct and there was no doubt about it. If somebody said he lost his leg and we see that he's without a leg, we didn't need to call the hospital to check out. But whenever there were any doubts, we did check it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was there a requirement that a person who was saying that he was under the command of, let's say, a particular person, that his commander would have to file a certification that he indeed was under his command and did -- was injured in the way that he described in the questionnaire?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that the witness be shown Exhibit 391, tab 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It also should be on the monitor in front of you. After you arrived in The Hague, in consultation with members of the Office of the Prosecutor, was this -- just a second -- was this chart created as an aid to the Chamber, identifying all the different types of records that make up a typical file in the fund?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 391, tab 3. It will not be put on the monitor. It does contain some confidential medical information regarding one of the applicants, so I would ask that this be tendered under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And I would ask, Mr. Vasiljkovic, would you take a look at the document the usher has here. And would it be fair to say that that is a summary of the paperwork contained in one particular file, the file of Jovan Vejnovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, over the course of the last year, did you permit copies of all of the documents in the fund to be made and put onto CDs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, the work of the fund is absolutely open to the public, and it is accessible to any organisation. We have a very extensive archives with some 67.000 files, and several organisations have already copied those documents, and I allowed you to do so as well, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I ask that the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit tab 1. These are 11 compact disks. I would note that the Prosecution is not seeking to tender these but is seeking simply to ask some foundational questions regarding them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Earlier this week were you asked to view the contents of these disks and to verify that they are indeed an accurate copy of the records of the fund?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did review them, and I have no reason to doubt anything. Of course, I couldn't look through each and every file - it would take years - but I'm satisfied and there is no doubt in my mind that they are not authentic and trustworthy, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The translation said that they are not authentic. Could you please restate --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say that again. I reviewed the documents. I was not able to review each file, because for that I would need several years. But as much as I was able to review, I am satisfied and I have no reason to doubt that these are not original documents. I have no reason to doubt -- the documents are original, in my opinion. They are original documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you place your initials on each of the CDs after you reviewed the CD?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I am going to tender a few specific records. I'm going to show them to you at this time. I'm going to ask that you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, before you go on, would you assist us with the relevance of this to the case. I'm not sure I'm following that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Perhaps I should have asked an additional question. If I could do that I think it may become clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljkovic, would it be fair to say that the documents contained in the Captain Dragan Fund would be a reliable source of information regarding where combatants were injured and fighting in both Bosnia and Croatia, including who their commander was, where they were injured, and how they were injured?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We have people from the whole of the territory of the former Yugoslavia. There were -- the fewest numbers were from Belgrade. Hardly any, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So, for example, if later in the trial a particular person be coming under -- in a special unit testified that he was injured in a particular place in Bosnia, the Chamber could take a look at these CDs to either verify or contradict the veracity of that statement. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With a high degree of certainty, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is there anything else the Chamber would wish me to ask in this regard?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask that you take a look at the screen in front of you, and this is a particular questionnaire, again of Vejnovic. I'd ask you to look at it, and I would ask you to tell us, from the questionnaire, where was his place of his enlistment and the date of his enlistment.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. 8th of August, 1992. I really can't read it. [Interpretation] Can I have a hard copy, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: For the record, this is tab 4 of 391.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. He joined -- [Interpretation] Pardon. He joined in the unit on the 8th of August, 1992. He joined the Knindza. [In English] It's called Knindza.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Who is his commander?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zika Crnogorac, or the Montenegrin.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And how was he injured?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours. Your Honours. In my submission, these files, recorded in this way, were served on the amici on Monday. I don't know when exactly Slobodan Milosevic received them, but these thousands and thousands of pages were served on us on Monday, and I think this is something the Court should be aware of. That is, on the 17th of this month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We will be looking into the question of disclosure and service, but for the moment, it doesn't affect the witness's evidence. He can give it, and then we'll consider what should be done with these records.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: May I just say, Your Honour, that the Prosecution is not tendering them, the disks now. The reason I'm asking these foundational questions is that, in the event some of these records become relevant later on in the trial, we won't -- it will not be necessary to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. have Mr. Vasiljkovic return to authenticate them. I imagine that there will be very few of these records that are actually tendered during the course of the trial. The five records that are being tendered today have been turned over in compliance with the discovery regime that was established for this witness. So there's no violation of the discovery for the actual exhibits that are being tendered today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So you are not seeking to exhibit anything beyond what we have, but on the other hand, you want to be in a position, if you need to, to be able to use them if matters arise later.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And equally, the amici or Mr. Milosevic may find that, after reviewing these CDs, that there is information that they would want to bring to the Chamber's attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I suppose the question does arise as to why this wasn't disclosed before.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The regime established for this witness, Your Honour, was one of delayed disclosure, and it was disclosed under that regime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just to add one point, Your Honour, because it is important: It's the volume of the material. It's over 10.000 pages on these CDs that has to be accessed in a special way which came to my possession yesterday. Mr. Tapuskovic had it first, it being largely in B/C/S, for us to look at. It's the volume that is so phenomenal. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We understand, and it is a matter which we are going to have to consider. It may be that in due course what we can do is to have at least the names of those whose records appear here, for ease of all, rather than having to read them all yourselves - an impossible task - it may be that we can get a list of the names, at least, and have that served.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution is in the process of generating such a list. The list will consist of the name of the person, the command that they said they were under, as well as the date and place of their injury; those key pieces of information. And we will make that available as soon as that list is completed. That is in process now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let's continue with this witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask you now -- that the witness be shown the certification from this particular file, and that is also tab 4 of Prosecution Exhibit 391. And if the usher could show the witness the hard copy. I believe the lights are making it difficult to read the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is this a typical certification that could be found in a claimant's file in the Captain Dragan Fund?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask you to read the first paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Certificate confirming that Jovan Vejnovic was born on the 19th of June, 1963 in Subotica, residing in Futog, Romanijska Street number 44," telephone number, et cetera. "Jovan Vejnovic is a member of the special unit for special purposes of the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia. "Carrying out that assignment of patrol --"

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's sufficient. I'm going to ask you now to take a look at Prosecution Exhibit 391, tab 5, the records of a person by the name of Sinisa Calic. I'm sorry, before the -- can the witness please have the certification. Can you tell us the signature on that certification, who -- this is tab 4, the one that you just read from. Whose signature is that on that page?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unit commander Zivojin Ivanovic, Crnogorac.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going back to tab 5, Sinisa Calic's file. Can you tell us what unit he belonged to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was -- he joined the unit on the 17th of July, 1991, a reconnaissance unit, a scouts unit, a special unit, Captain Dragan, under contract. That was his status at the time. He was wounded near Skabrnja in 1993, under my command.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe for us, what does "soldier on contract" mean?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that in 1992 or 1993, the beginning of 1993, before I came there, the Serbian army of Krajina carried out a reorganisation, engaging soldiers on contract. They had begun some sort of professionalisation, and he was one of such soldiers. And he was wounded when I arrived there. He was given to me, to my unit, and he was wounded in the battle for Skabrnja under my command.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd ask that you be shown, from the same exhibit, this certification in the file, and I would simply ask you to tell us who -- who verified his injury and his place of injury.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rade Bozic. He was then in charge of the centre that I established, and he came back again to help me set up a similar centre in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The stamp that appears next to Mr. Bozic's name, can you help us by identifying that stamp?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a standard stamp of the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, the official stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to now draw your attention to tab 6 of Prosecution Exhibit 391, the records, or some of the records, of a person by the name of Miodrag Obradovic. I want to first ask you about the questionnaire. Can you please read the relevant portion of the record that identifies how Mr. Obradovic was wounded.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 24th of May, 1992, in Brcko, Klanac, during the attack on a Ustasha house, he was shot at and wounded in his right low -- in his right upper arm. He was captured on the 30th of June, 1992, where he suffered serious physical injuries. I can't read the couple of words that follow. And after that, he was in hospital in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you now to read from the portion of the record that indicates what he expresses as his intention to do after he is discharged from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The translation that we have in the exhibit is "right lower leg," but it appears it should be "upper arm." Mr. Groome, perhaps someone could check that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We'll check that translation and -- we'll have it checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljkovic, can you assist us on that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. My mistake. The Judge is right, it's right lower leg. I don't know why I'm reading this in the first place. Why doesn't your translator read it out? I didn't write this, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm just asking you to read from the records, as the administrator of the fund, to read from the Serbian records kept in the fund. I draw your attention to the portion of the record where Mr. Obradovic states his intention -- his intentions after he recuperates. Can you please read that section of the record.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The wounded returned from the battlefield." It's really difficult for me to read this handwriting because it's not a simple one to make out, and I would really ask somebody to help me with it. I can't make out --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljkovic --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- one in two words.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We will perhaps ask the translator to read it. Can you verify that this is a record from the Captain Dragan Fund? Can you do that from your examination of the document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask that the witness be shown the certification from the same file, and I would simply ask you, do you recognise the signature of the person who certificated this man's injury, and if you can assist us in identifying the stamp over the signature.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here "Captain Bozic," and the stamp is the military stamp of the Brcko region.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the stamp from the Brcko region, does it identify -- is this a JNA stamp or a Ministry of Interior stamp? Are you able to tell us that from looking at the stamp?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is a JNA stamp because it has the five -- five-cornered star and it has the number of the military post box. It's 984.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There are only two more records I'd seek your comment on. I'd ask you to take a look at Prosecution Exhibit 391, tab 7, the certificate submitted in the case of Mr. Ranko Strbac. I ask you, do you recognise who signed this certification?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here Zeljko Raznjatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the stamp that accompanies Zeljko Raznjatovic's name, do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I see this. I never noticed it before. Territorial Defence centre, the command in Erdut, which probably means that this Zeljko Raznjatovic was under the command of this Territorial Defence centre in Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, this letter signed by Raznjatovic, how does it indicate this person was injured; where and when?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean I should find this place in the document if I read it in its entirety? "Certificate and confirmation of wounding --"

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No need to read out loud. If you could scan it and just identify the portion of it that indicates where and when this person was injured, according to Mr. Raznjatovic. Mr. Raznjatovic is Arkan; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could you just indicate -- where does Arkan say this man was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. injured?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slavonia-Baranja-Western Srem, Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask you to look at the screen in front of you. This is a portion of the document highlighted. I'd ask you just to read that one portion. Does that indicate where Arkan said this man was injured?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find it here. I'm really trying. I don't see it mentioned specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We don't need it read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I just want to draw your attention to the last sentence of the letter from Arkan, the certification. Can you please read the last letter, where it begins, "It is our opinion..."

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "It is our opinion that all conditions have been met for disability status for an invalid of war according to the Article 97, paragraph 2, Law on Basic Rights of Invalids of War and the Families of the Deceased," Official Gazette number and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This last sentence, is this Arkan stating his belief that the federal law as it regarded war invalids applied to his men?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe he's saying that this refers to -- yes. Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The last document I'm going to ask you to take a look at is tab 8 of Prosecution Exhibit 392. The Chamber will be able to read the entirety of the document. I just want you to read for us the disposition of this case; what payments were made by the Captain Dragan Fund to this person.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certificate confirming that -- this is a very bad copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The certificate. Who signed the certificate for this man, Mr. Vukan Subaric?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zeljko Raznjatovic. In fact, it says Zeljko Raznjatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, please look at the disposition on the last page of the questionnaire, and that's the ERN ending 063, and it's up on the screen now. The portion beginning: "I suggest paying the amount of 5.000 dinars ..."

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "With the proviso that --" I have a little problem with this lighting and the reflection from the monitor. These are very bad copies, and I have trouble reading this handwriting. It is not the best of handwritings anyway. Will you please find a translator who will read this out better than I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll read the translation for you and ask you to comment on it. "I suggest paying the amount of 5.000 dinars to the patient. His wife will bring medical insurance cards for their children, as they will get 100.000 -- or 100 dinars per child, the 15th of July, 1992. The patient has asked for financial support. He was instructed to submit a document confirming that he is unemployed. The case is settled because the municipality will take care about the patient." Assuming that that is a correct translation of the record in the fund, does that indicate that in this particular instance, one of Arkan's men who was injured received official benefits from the municipality in which he lived?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that later, laws were passed according to which all people who were victims of war benefited from one or another form of aid. Not only these men but everyone else. You could read that in newspapers. It is no major discovery.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to return to the video that we watched last -- yesterday, and I want to ask you to comment on a few particular sections of that video. If you would look at the screen in front of you. The person that we are viewing on the screen now --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see anything. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If we could have the sound, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The person who greeted Mr. Milosevic and presented the troops for inspection, is the name that was listed in the transcript, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Milorad Lukovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milorad Lukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I believe "Vukelic" was in the transcript. Does Mr. Lukovic have another name that he's popularly known as?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had a nickname. It was "Legija." I believe he also had another nickname, "Ulemek," that was linked to him at a certain period.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I draw your attention to the monitor in front of you at 8:36 on the video. Mr. Stanisic is laying a wreath at a memorial to a Mr. Kostic. Can you just tell the Chamber what, if anything, you know about who this person Mr. Kostic was.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, although I can't put my money on it, that I met with him once in Belgrade before his killing, but the Tribunal itself can draw the conclusion that he was an important person in the state security service, and he was one of the first people to get killed in the fighting in that war. Nothing very important. I think he was linked with a completely different theatre of war, and I had no major contacts with Kostic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask you to look at another still from the video. This person Rade Bozovic, the person who Mr. Milosevic is saying, "I've read those reports of yours," can you tell us what, if anything, you know about who Mr. Bozovic is and where he was engaged.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He appeared at the fortress a couple of days after my arrival from Glina, so I had little time to spend with him. He was also at Fruska Gora when the establishment of JCO began, or when the planning for the establishment of the JCO began. And later, I would meet him around town, but we had no special business or any other contacts or common projects.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to now play a few excerpts from the speech made by Frenki Simatovic and ask for your comment on some portions of.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: [Please refer to Exhibit 390, tab 2 for video transcript - 05:56]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Simatovic talks about the 4th of May, 1991, as the date on which this unit was founded. Does that date have any significance to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I established my company on the 4th of April, so it can't be linked with me. It must have concerned some internal decisions of theirs for the establishment of that unit. I can only guess that this is so, but I really wasn't the sort of person to whom they would report about their activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljkovic, you've been using an abbreviation for this unit which has been recorded as JCO. Is that the abbreviation that you intend or is there some problem of mishearing what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Special Operations Unit, JSO.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that this unit became to be known as the JSO around the time of the ceremony that we saw yesterday?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I attended a similar celebration two years previously. Maybe names changed in the meantime, but in my mind, that unit had been established or had begun to be established at the time we went to Fruska Gora. As far as I remember, that's what we always called it, but I really can't be sure now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. We ask that you watch the next portion of the speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: [Please refer to Exhibit 390, tab 2 for video transcript - 08:22]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In that portion, Mr. Simatovic says that they were forced to operate in complete secrecy. When you trained your men and in the battle of Glina and Ljubovo, were your men trained to conceal that they were associated with you and your unit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. I really don't understand your question at all. What does the secrecy of the service has to do with it? It works in secret because it is a secret service. If it were a public service, it would be working in public. And what does my unit have to do with it? And the way you are putting your question is really -- eludes my understanding. Would you please split your question in two.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes. My apologies. At the time that you conducted your training, during any part of your training did you train your men -- now, I'm not associating your men with what Mr. Simatovic is saying, I'm asking you, did you train your men to conceal their association with the Knindza?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were a police unit that had its own uniforms, its flag, its base, its headquarters. We were a public service. And as far as I understand, this other unit is part of the secret service. And I really don't see the point of all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to look at another portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: [Please refer to Exhibit 390, tab 2 for video transcript - 09:33]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In this particular portion, Mr. Simatovic is estimating the amount of soldiers at 5.000 and telling his audience that it was coordinated by the unit command and intelligence team from the second administration. Could you comment on any relationship you're aware of between the JSO and the second administration?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again you're asking me two or three questions at once and I find it very difficult to answer when you do that, so I'd like you to ask me more specific questions. But since you're asking me, I think it's high Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. time that we say some things: That this staged performance that we all attended was prepared to welcome the president. In his report, he mentions Benkovac, Glina -- I don't have the exact transcript, I'd like to read it again. But first of all, in Benkovac there were no operations or fighting. Kostajnica was taken without a single shot being fired. And Frenki probably didn't know about it until he read it out in the papers. So it was prepared for the president, to give an impression on him. What does the president know where Kostajnica or where Benkovac is or what happened there? So I quite understand that. So this unit never exceeded the size of a company. I don't know where he got the figure of 5.000 from, but I have absolutely no evidence to that effect. This was for the public. This was a theatre performance. I even asked him later on, "Where did you get all those numbers from?" He said, "I didn't write it all. I just gave some instructions, but we have to embellish it a little bit for the benefit of the president." So I don't think you can take this to be a reliable document. You had thousands of observers and monitors in Krajina. Did anyone ever mention 5.000 or anything like that? It is so exaggerated here. Believe me, I've been here for two weeks now, and maybe I'm getting towards the end of my tether a little bit, but their participant is really over exaggerated that I feel ashamed to take part in this. This has nothing to do with the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Counsel may have his purpose in answering a question -- or asking a question. Answer it as best you can. If you can't answer, just say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljkovic, are you saying that all of the statements that Mr. Simatovic said, and I'll just summarise them here: Where Mr. Simatovic talks about an air helicopter squadron that transported tons of equipment and materials into Bosnia; then when Mr. Simatovic talks about 26 training camps for special police units of Republika Srpska, Republic of Serbian Krajina; that when Mr. Simatovic talks about the involvement of these forces in freeing the UNPROFOR hostages; that all of these are mistruths or lies or gross exaggerations of the truth? Is that what you're saying here this morning?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't say that. Far from it. I'm just saying that what he said in connection with the Krajina, and that is the only area I can comment on with certainty, I am saying that Mr. Simatovic or his men had nothing to do with Glina or Kostajnica or Benkovac. Nothing ever happened there in that sense. And as for helicopter units, I know of two Gazelles and one Bell from the Vietnam war which he had at his disposal. But as this is a gentleman who liked planes, he spoke about it as a helicopter squadron. I have friends who own more helicopters than that. So all this is absolutely exaggerated. I don't think there's any material evidence to corroborate this. As for UNPROFOR, we are aware of that, but I do not wish to comment on anything that was done in Kosovo or Bosnia. I don't know. But what did happen in Krajina, I knew about it at least while I was in command there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I direct your attention to a map that was seen in the video. It's on the screen in front of you. Can you tell us what, if anything, you can tell us about this map and any indications that are on it.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I think this was done in copper. It was a work of art of a sculptor who was a friend of the unit who worked on their insignia and everything else, but I don't think it's anything of any major importance. This is a map of the former Yugoslavia, and it was made with a great deal of nostalgia, in copper. It is the work of an artist, not of a strategist or commander. As far as I remember. I may be wrong. I see Mr. Milosevic looking at it close up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to draw your attention now to tab 5 of Prosecution Exhibit 390. You've seen this exhibit yesterday. It was the stills from the video and your correction of people that were incorrectly identified. I just want to draw your attention to page 062, time frame 04:50. Could you please identify the two people in that still of the video.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mihalj Kertes and General Zivota Panic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I draw your attention to 07:55 of the video. Tell us who is in this still.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jovica Stanisic, Slobodan Milosevic, and Milorad Lukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I draw your attention to the next page and the time stamp 15:41. Can you please identify these people for us.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vucelic, Tepavcevic, Vasiljevic, and Lukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could you tell us; Mr. Vucelic, who is he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know him as director of RTS, and I think he was an official in the SPS party while it was in power. I think he has his own party now. That's as much as I know about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In an earlier portion -- or I'm sorry, a portion of the video after this, Mr. Stanisic presents three gifts to three people, Mr. Milosevic, Mr. Kertes, and is this the Mr. Vucelic who is presented the third gift?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember. It didn't seem so important to me for me to remember it. Probably, yes. A lot of people were given awards. I think so. I think you're right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I ask you to take a look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just the picture before. 15:41, the picture previous.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we'll call that up now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Number 3 man, he called this General Vasiljevic. Is this Aleksandar Vasiljevic, the previous witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you know or have any personal contact with General Aleksandar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had no need to have any contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Had you ever personally met him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, if I hadn't seen this tape, I wouldn't have even remembered that he was at this ceremony. He didn't mean anything to me. I had no contact with him, so I really don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The next still I'm going -- I'm sorry. The one before, the Mr. Paskovic, I believe the name was, the second man. Who is he? Tepavcevic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tepavcevic was a high-ranking official in the state security who died last year or the year before.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The next portion I'd like you to look at is the time stamp 23:23. And who is in this frame?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Rajh, and I am next to him. That's me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And finally --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you like to know who Mr. Rajh is?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, please. Tell us who he is.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Rajh, I met him as one of the suppliers who purchased some supplies for the service, and that is how he introduced himself to me. He's Frenki Simatovic's Kum or best man. I know that for certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I draw your attention now to 24 minutes, the still from that time. Can you describe who is depicted in this still.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Is my monitoring playing up or --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could you please check his monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Push the "off" button.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay? Who is depicted in this particular still?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Jovica Stanisic and Milorad Vucelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And finally, the still at 30:28. And who is depicted in this still?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slobodan Milosevic and Milorad Vucelic. They're chatting, with drinks in their hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to look at final short excerpt. At the end of it, I would ask you, can you tell us who was the person making the toast?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: [Please refer to Exhibit 390, tab 2 for video transcript - 39:14]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Who is the person who made the toast?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zivojin Ivanovic, known as Zika Crnogorac, the Montenegrin.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Vasiljkovic continued to live in the former Yugoslavia during times relevant to the Chamber's inquiry. He was well-known in the region from 1991 onwards, and there is a large volume of material from contemporaneous media and other sources which refers to him which the Prosecution has not been able to further investigate. There is a volume of documents and reports which, if believed, would be in direct conflict with his testimony as to events after the period with which he's already testified. All of this material has been provided to the amici and the accused under Rule 68, and they may wish to explore this material at length. I, however, in light of my obligations as an attorney and a prosecutor, will conclude my examination at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. It's for you to cross-examine. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Captain, do you know that in this institution you are listed as a protected witness, B-073? That is your pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't insist on that. I asked that everything be in public.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you at any point in time wish or ask or in any way made it known that you wanted to testify anonymously rather than in public?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. God forbid. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did a member of the opposing side, I think -- I refer to the fake Prosecution, did he suggest to you that you should testify confidentially and that you have protection?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I learnt about it for the first time when I arrived here, and I said that I didn't want any protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they asked you whether you wanted to be a protected witness?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's me be quite frank. It was like this: I arrived, and I said that I had made a statement to the media saying that I was coming here, and then they said, "Aren't you a protected witness?" And I said, "As far as I know, I am not." "Yes, but we've listed you as a protected witness." And I said I didn't know anything about that. So that's all I know about this question of protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you had nothing to conceal from the public, nor do you have anything now, and you have no reason, nor did you have any reason, nor did you make any requests at any time to be anonymous here or in any proceedings or any testimony, and whatever I ask you can also be done in public?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I wish to draw your attention to this. The previous witness was in a similar situation, though he was, to some extent, protected. This one is quite different. But this is the umpteenth time that the opposite side is keeping the witness under a pseudonym as a protected witness to prevent me from collecting facts, and the witness is claiming that he never requested any kind of protection and that he never wanted to be an anonymous witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this is a gross abuse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have your point. Now, Mr. Nice, if I can address you on this subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The accused is right that this is the second occasion of two witnesses of which this has occurred, and it's not the first time. There have been other witnesses during this trial. Now, this really is a matter of concern, because it appears -- now, I may be wrong, but it appears that the Prosecution is of its own decision putting these matters forward, or else the witness isn't right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In respect of both these witnesses, I'll need a little bit more time to research the detailed history. I'll come back to you with it, if I may, a little later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. And would you do that, and would you review your practice in relation to future witnesses to ensure it doesn't happen if it has been happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's already in my mind and I hope in our practice, but I will review these two and come back to you before the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the amicus filed an observation on this matter with the Registry yesterday as a matter for the attention of the Trial Chamber, principally in relation to the last witness and previous examples. So we've put it in a paper form already. It might be appropriate if the Prosecution provided a report in response as to the exact dealings with this witness and the previous witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may just add --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We haven't -- we haven't yet got your observations, and it may be it's in the machine somewhere, in the bureaucracy. Maybe if you had a copy available for us we could look at it sometime today before the Prosecution reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nice, if you would do that at the end of the day. I have in mind we have to deal with at least one witness today, General Mangan, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. And there may be matters I need to raise about that witness as well. I'll see. So a few minutes at the end of the day will be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we'll have to stop at half past one. I take it there's another case this afternoon. Mr. Milosevic, we will take up the matters you raise. Now, let us continue with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope you will, Mr. May. But I would like to draw your attention to the fact that this is not the second case but the umpteenth case, because more than half of the protected witnesses were later unprotected, and we'll make up the exact statistics and we'll see what it is about. I claim it is a manipulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Captain, do you have anything to add in connection with these tricks over protection, non-protection, your possible requests? Have you omitted to say anything about this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just wanted to say that I didn't even accept this type of protection that they issue in a routine way, which I refused to sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what that is.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] "This is to confirm a commitment of the part of a Prosecutor that any conversation or statement you will make during the course of your preparation to testify as a witness in the case of Prosecutor versus Milosevic will not be used against you." [Interpretation] I think that everything should be used against me that I do which is wrong. If I give false testimony, I should be held accountable too. So I didn't wish to sign this either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. That's rather interesting, and I think it is a good thing for the public to be aware of such documents issued by the other side that you call the Prosecution, that everything is stated -- that is stated here against me cannot be used against the person making such a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's not an accurate reading of that document. Under Rules 42 and 43, in order for the Prosecution to put the allegations that it was in possession of to Mr. Vasiljkovic, we had one of two choices: One, to tape record the entire proceeding and furnish transcripts, or the other way, which is the proffer, to give him a guarantee that he could answer, respond to allegations that we put to him honestly, without fear of their later being used against him. It was a mechanism to comply with Rules 42 and 43, as well as to give Mr. Vasiljkovic a further assurance that he could be completely honest and open in his discussions and responses to allegations of specific criminal conduct put to him during the course of his preparation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljkovic, I haven't mentioned so far, but so that you understand the legal position, you do not have to answer any questions which you think may incriminate you. If you wish to object to such questions, you can do so to the Trial Chamber. But that merely -- I know your position; I'm merely telling you what your legal position is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You have to clarify something for me, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Isn't this in collusion with this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You mustn't ask me questions. All I'm doing is telling you what your legal position is. You are not obliged to answer any questions which may incriminate you. So you can decline to answer. It doesn't affect the declaration you've taken.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You're also a citizen of Australia, are you not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you completed military schools over there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I heard that you said yesterday that you worked for six years in the army of Australia, as an instructor of various formations in Latin America, Africa, Kuwait?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not quite so. They added these things. After Australia, I went to Africa. I worked in Africa as a security advisor. Then the air force academy I worked as a flying instructor and as a sailing instructor too. So I was an instructor of some sort all my life, and I think this paid in Krajina, and that is probably why I did my job well. So my experience is in Australia, a little in Africa. It was more to do with security than military. And my experience in Krajina, which was unbelievable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In any event, we can say that you can competently assess military operations, military organisation, operations on the ground, and everything that was happening in the areas in which you were present, that you are professionally trained for that and that you have the necessary experience to qualify you to judge about these things competently.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that that was at the strategic level, but at the tactical level, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I will certainly not put any questions to you beyond the tactical level or which are not specifically linked to your activities.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But before we start with those questions, would you tell me, please, whether for your appearance in The Hague in the capacity as a witness, did you receive any money from the opposing party?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So far I have received about 4.000 euros. I have to explain that most of that money was spent for the tickets, because I came here from Africa, and for hotel accommodation, because I have spent some time here. I hope you don't think that they can buy me for 4.000 euros.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No. I don't doubt that. I'm just asking whether anything was offered.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Just to cover my expenses. And I received about 4.000 euros.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is all you received from them, for your travelling expenses and accommodation costs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us clear up a few more points. You were mentioned here by certain witnesses, and I assume you followed some of that, probably not all of it. You were linked to the state security service of the Republic of Serbia. You were described as a mercenary. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am. I know quite a lot. Probably not all of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, please will you give me a direct and very categorical answer: Did you ever officially or unofficially, directly or indirectly, were you ever a member of the State Security Service of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In two cases. Once on an honourary basis in 1997 for 28 days when I was engaged, together with 20 observers, to monitor exercises. And I received 2.200 dinars there as a fee. I wrote out my report, and I was engaged on that basis by them. And the second occasion was there was some discussion that I would be engaged in the future, and that engagement was linked to Fruska Gora. It lasted some ten days or maybe a fortnight, and it never came about. It was discussed, but it was never realised. So those were the only two occasions when I may have been in a position to receive orders from anyone from the state security service. Those were the two occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The fact that you were engaged to monitor exercises of the police, this was in 1997 or 1996?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This was somewhere near Nis, according to my notes. It was in Serbia, near Nis?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was just waiting because the interpreters. Yes, close to Nis somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this was in 1996?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, in 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. So you were engaged because they considered you to be a qualified professional to be able to assess their military exercises?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you were engaged, you were hired as a professional and not as a member of the service. So at the time you were not a member of the service either, were you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you never were a member of the State Security Service of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. I was never a member of the service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's time for an adjournment. We will adjourn now. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Captain, during your stay in Krajina, you were a member of the defence units of the SAO Krajina. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was down there two times. The first time I was a member of the Krajina police, and the second time I was a member of the Krajina army. You have to understand that at the beginning, when the defence efforts began, they began with the people organised by the Martic police. So in the first part of the war in 1991, I was under the command of Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understand that. But doubtlessly from what you say, the Krajina police and the Serbian army of Krajina both constitute the defence forces of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So in all your posts, you were a member of those forces.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you were under the command of the defence forces of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: During your stay in Krajina and all those activities you testified about, did you receive any order at all from a person who was a member of the state security service in the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive your salary during your service in Krajina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not a dinar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So let's clear this up: Could we say that you were a mercenary in Krajina or, as you testify here, your motives were completely different? As I understand them, they were absolutely patriotic in nature. They were not mercenary. You did not work there for lucrative purposes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, in the first paragraph, and I will quote you: "In the military sense, Krajina was ruled by complete chaos. It was a time of massive emigration of Serbian refugees to Knin." Do you remember that that -- that at that time there was a large number of Serbian refugees coming into Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid this is a mistake, because what I said was there was a massive flow of Serbian refugees to Belgrade from Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you agree. Do you remember that in that first year we already had about 100.000 refugees from various areas of Croatia, not only from Krajina, in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that, but I know that there were very few people in Knin. Most of them had left to Serbia, and I don't know any figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you go on in the same paragraph: "In the hearts of the Serbian people, there was great fear, and the generally accepted opinion was that these people should be defended." Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in your opinion, what was the reason for this fear in the hearts and minds of Serbs that made them flee from the territory of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without wishing to go too deep into history, as far as I followed, a lot has been said here already, but you have to understand -- and it's probably very difficult for someone who lived in the West, and I was lucky enough to live both in the West and in Serbia and in Krajina, and I can understand how difficult it is for the Trial Chamber to understand that this is a relatively poor people who lived in small houses -- I'm talking about rural areas now. They lived in small rooms on the upper floor without any TV sets. Stories circulated about atrocities from the Second World War and the stories became more and more horrible with retelling. And then came the appearance of Ustasha uniforms and the chequerboard flag. That very word "chequerboard flag" inspired great fear in every Serb. There is almost not a single family which does not have in its history a great tragedy. It's not such a long time. We're talking about 50 years. There are people still alive who remember all that. And it is clear to everyone who made the smallest effort to follow those events that all those people were very afraid from this spectre of fascism rising again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's very clear. In paragraph 5, you say: "Among the volunteers, there was a general willingness to fight this revived fascism, the resurgent fascism."

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say: "There were no great idealists among us, and the future did not seem rosy to us."

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I say something? If I can say in my on words how I saw it. A person who lies in the bed of his ancestors who had been there for 600 years and wakes up turning into a potential minority from being a constituent nation, so he wakes up as a potential minority under a government which promises him expulsions, slaughter, killings -- [In English] They didn't have a rosy future.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But quite briefly and concisely, we could say perhaps, and you will confirm this or not, that it is precisely this resurgent fascism of the new Croatian authorities was the reason why the Serbian people in Croatia were afraid.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. There's no dilemma about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's move on then, Captain. Did anyone at all invite you to come or did anyone send you to Krajina, or did you feel yourself that it was your patriotic duty to defend that people there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I felt myself that I could help and that my help could save lives. That was my primary motive. I don't think any one of us here could sit in this chair if they knew that if they went out they could save lives. I don't think that's something exceptional. It's the normal drive and wish of a person to do whatever they can. And it is a fact that by going there I did save lives. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. And you heard from Sasa Medakovic, who was the prime initiator of my going to the Krajina, the main reason for my going there was my own feeling that I should. Today nobody could even prevent me from going there. Even you would not have been able to prevent me if I had really felt the need to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You just mentioned Sasa Medakovic. That is a man from Krajina and he lived in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. And he died in Krajina. He was killed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he was born, lived, and got killed in Krajina defending his people from Ustashas?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We heard claims here that Franko Simatovic, and to some extent Jovica Stanisic, according to Babic's testimony, were in charge of this camp in Golubic. There was even some talk about Franko Simatovic being the commander of that camp. Is it true that during your stay in Krajina you were the exclusive commander of the camp in Golubic, or was there a time when it was somebody else?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was the only commander, and no one else could have occupied that post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that you were appointed commander of that camp by somebody from the state security service of Serbia, or was it someone from Krajina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan Martic, with the approval of Milan Babic who was the supreme authority at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you were appointed by the legal chief of the Krajina police, Martic, with the approval of the then president of the Krajina government, Babic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did the state security service or anyone else from Serbia in the broadest sense have anything to do with your appointment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. That claim can absolutely not stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it is not in dispute that at the first stage when you were a member of the police of Krajina and carried out your duties in that capacity, whereas later you were a member of the Serbian army of Krajina within the framework of the command system of the Krajina armed forces, meaning both the police and the army, not Serbia and not the JNA. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is so, and I believe that is fully corroborated by the existing documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true - you said something about that - that the attitude of a significant number of the members of the people in the Republic of Serbian Krajina was almost hostile to JNA members?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. There was a number of factions. In fact, factions had begun to emerge.
