To me, as someone who came from outside, trying to help -- and when I say "outside," don't forget that to me Knin, Krajina, Rijeka, Ljubljana, those were cities in my own country to me. But when I came there, I noticed a significant difference; various factions between Martic and Babic. There were different currents there. So they were on the one hand, and the army on the other hand, which was completely untouchable. And as soon as I spoke, as I exchanged my first word with the JNA officer, that was in June, whereas I arrived in April, to that extent was the army removed. And it was easier for me to cooperate with the UNPROFOR than with the JNA. It's a shame, but that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say again in paragraph 8: "The JNA was completely unimportant. We didn't inform them of anything. They were close by between two sides, and we didn't know how they would react." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because at that time there were Croats, Macedonians, Slovenes, all ethnicities in the army, in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that such an attitude to the JNA is explained by the fact that the JNA, at the time, treated both sides equally and almost without exception tried to play a buffer between those Croat paramilitary formations and the Serbian members of territorial units and civilians?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since the 5th Command of the army was stationed in Zagreb, I felt personally that the army was against the Serbs. Now, looking back, I can agree, perhaps, with you that it was neutral, but at that time I believed that the army that was stationed in Glina was not really kindly disposed to Serbs. But if you look at it this way, you can say that the army was much more conscientious in holding the line between the Serbs and the Croats than certain forces of the UNPROFOR, at least in my experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And from your experience again, I'm speaking about that time again, about events which were the result of these pressures on the Serbs from these paramilitary formations, is it true that Croat officers and soldiers increasingly deserted from the JNA, taking with them their weapons in order to join Croat paramilitary formations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is common knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in fact, the greatest number of officers of the 5th Army deserted at that time.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's mainly Croats that served in the 5th Army. So you can't say that the army was on my side, because I was the only one carrying out operations at the time. And it is true, yes, most of them deserted in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understood from your testimony that you were quite concerned and afraid that the JNA might take action against you, and you said that you held 60 per cent of your forces in a state of alert in case you were attacked by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, yes. And we did have a clash in Glina after the liberation of Glina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me now again from your experience, if it had happened - I'm not saying it did - but if you with your forces had attacked JNA members, do you believe that the JNA would have retaliated in defence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They absolutely would have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when attacked by Croatian forces, is it true that they only returned fire and did not commit any acts of aggression against the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my assessment, they had much more strength and capacity to retaliate than they actually used. And if I had been in their shoes, I would have retaliated much more strongly when they were in the position in which they were, when their barracks were blockaded, when their people were attacked, when their men were in danger. But that's my assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that at the cost of sacrifices, casualties, and humiliation, they tried to minimise their reactions and reacted just as much as was necessary to protect the garrisons that were under attack?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is absolutely fair to say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Talking about the people who made up the defence of Krajina, in the beginning it was only the police, the Territorial Defence, and later, the Serbian army of Krajina. Is it true that those were precisely people from Krajina, and only in individual cases were they volunteers from Serbia who arrived as individuals or groups?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the very beginning, until July, perhaps, I believe you can count on the fingers of one hand the volunteers who accidentally found their way into Krajina. There were no other people except natives of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At any time during your stay in Krajina, and you were there until 1994, with interruptions --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until 1995, until the fall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At any time was there a unit of the MUP of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If you give me two minutes --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only men who set their foot there from the MUP of Serbia, as far as I know, and I believe I know a lot, were Jovica Stanisic once on an informal visit; Frenki Simatovic three or four times. Let's make it five. I saw him only in the beginning. Milan Radonjic who spent a total of three days there. Milan Radonjic, I mentioned him before. And Dragan Filipovic whom I also saw three or four times. In my view, what were they doing there? They were collecting intelligence. We're talking about four men. One, two, three, four. Year 1991, where there were no computers in sight. The first computer appeared in Krajina in 1993. What could they have been doing? I don't know what Jovica is by training. Is he a political worker or a lawyer? There were two men working for the service, defectologists or social workers by training, and one computer scientist who didn't even graduate. That's Frenki. Their presence there was so exaggerated. Mr. Milosevic, thousands of observers passed through Krajina. I don't believe you will find -- I believe this Tribunal has many of their reports, and there are many reports about me. I don't believe you will find a single report mentioning a fifth person. And believe me when I say that there are many people, many more people working here in the Tribunal today whom I saw here who had been in Krajina. If you have the impression that I am being protective towards Frenki, you will be right. I knew him. We were friends. Somebody said so a moment -- a moment ago, "You were friends and he was your superior." That's true. I simply can't believe that this number of serious people is discussing four half-trained men --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Just a moment. Don't -- if you would, don't run on. Just concentrate on the question and try and deal with that. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Talking about these four men, I understand that you are not talking about their presence of any length there but only about their overall presence during that period of time, which can only be measured in a matter of days, two, three, or four days for all four of them.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that someone was there for three days. One day, two days maybe, but I can't say that any one of them spent more than three days there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So is it clear, then, that these four men, apart from having possible reasons of a private nature - as you know, Stanisic has relatives in the Krajina - that they were there exclusively to collect information and to study the situation, which was their job.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm absolutely convinced that that is so and that there were no conditions to do anything more than that. Especially if you have Babic against you, you have the JNA against you, you have all these factions against you. It was technically not possible to do anything more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Captain, I should like us to clear this up completely. Last night, on the Belgrade and Zagreb media, I saw a news report to the effect that you had here -- testified here that formations in Krajina were formed under the competence of the MUP or the DB of the Republic of Serbia. And as I understood you to say -- when you referred to MUP and DB, you were referring to the MUP and DB of the Krajina. When you're talking about the army, you're talking about the JNA and, after the withdrawal of the JNA, the Serbian army of Krajina. So is my understanding correct or is the understanding of the reporters who claim that you testified that the state security of Serbia had organised the military units in Krajina? Did they understand you better and inform the public accordingly? What was your testimony yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me make it plain: It doesn't matter what the reports say. What matters in this trial is what is said in the court and what the Trial Chamber decides about it. Now, what is being suggested here, or appears to be suggested by the accused, is that you are referring to the security service of Krajina and not that of Serbia. If you want the question clarified, we'll have him clarify it, but if you think you can answer it, do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I was speaking yesterday, I was speaking exclusively about the service of Krajina, the police of Krajina, or the army of Krajina and the JNA, or the JNA up until the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So I hope that matter is quite clear now, because you said no one could participate without the permission of either the service or the police or the army. Those were your words.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not questioning that. I just wanted to make quite clear the definition because of this kind of reporting and distorting what you say. When you say the service, you mean the state security of Krajina. When you say the army, you mean the army of Krajina. And when you say the police, you mean the police of Krajina. And you do not imply under any of these organisations, the police or the State Security Service of Serbia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 3, paragraph 4 of your statement, you say that when you arrived in Krajina, the state security of Krajina had already been formed. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. According to my understanding, yes, of course. Yes. Sasa Medakovic and other people were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you go on to say on page 3, paragraph 4, that in those days, you saw Frenki Simatovic in Knin only a couple of times and that you asked Sasa Medakovic, "Who is that man and who is Jovica Stanisic?" And he answered that they were from the Belgrade DB and that they wanted to remain incognito because their bosses didn't know they were there. This is stated on page 3, paragraph 4 of your statement; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. And they were not the only people who came there without their bosses knowing about it. Dr. Ivanovic, who took leave to come to Krajina to assist, and their superiors in the hospital didn't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Captain, it is without doubt that the state security of the Republic of Serbia and the state security of Krajina cooperated in a certain sense because they are related services. But is it true that you never received any order from, for instance, Frenki Simatovic or Jovica Stanisic regarding any military security or any other activity?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course that is true. It would be the same as if the porter were to give an order to the cook. I don't understand. There were no circumstances for them to give me orders. They knew nothing about what I was doing, nor were they qualified in my field of work. I told -- I said what their qualifications were in April 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Though I think we have established the very limited number of people that came there and the time they spent there, who came there to collect information mostly, do you know -- do you have any direct or indirect knowledge that they or anyone else from the state security of Serbia had initiated or suggested, not to say ordered, any crime to be committed in the territory of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: God forbid, no. Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 7, paragraph 3, and I quote: "Frenki appeared from time to time, but I find it hard to believe that he was Milosevic's man. I never heard him say any nice word about him." So could you infer then, or even today, that I had sent Frenki to Krajina, or did he go there simply as part of his professional duty, and he headed the intelligence work in the state security service?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite frank, I could never link Frenki to you and your political work. I grew up in a country in which we were not educated to respect political leaders too much. And in my presence, he never said anything for me to link him to you. I saw him as a member of the service who was professionally doing his work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 7, paragraph 3, you said that he saw himself as a professional agent in the struggle against terrorism rather than as a political figure of any kind. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you now since, regarding your testimony, I'm not quite clear on one point. Did I understand you correctly? You said that you saw Stanisic only twice in Knin, that he had relatives there. The second time you saw him when he allegedly came to relieve you of your duties. This was on page 7, paragraph 4. From your testimony, my impression is that this wasn't worded properly. He didn't come to relieve you of your duty, since you had clashed with Babic, who accused you of being a mercenary, and as Stanisic hadn't even appointed you to that position, he couldn't relieve you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw Stanisic only once. The second time -- I think this is a play of words in that paragraph. I will explain in a minute. I saw Stanisic for the second time in Belgrade, after this problem with Babic had arisen, when he told me that I shouldn't go back again. I did use the words "relieve me of my duties" because he made it known to me that I shouldn't go back there, but of course that doesn't mean that he had appointed me. Even the Patriarch Paul could have relieved me because he had influence over me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it was a suggestion on his part. We will come to the motives for such a suggestion later. When you speak of Babic on page 7, paragraph 10, you say that: "His problem was that I was seen as Martic's number one man, and he was Martic's political opponent. If he could harm me, he could harm Martic, and he would take control over the military forces in Krajina." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe it's my pride coming to the fore there, but really, yes, that's how I felt it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So is it true that Babic wanted at all cost to take over control over both the military and police forces in Krajina, to control everything that was going on in Krajina, in other words?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There's no dilemma on that score.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true, then, that it was really Milan Babic who expelled you from Krajina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My feeling was that Milan Babic was superior to you, that he had more authority, because if you had had authority over him, both Frenki and I would have stayed on in Krajina. At least, that is my opinion. However, that -- my intolerance towards you was that I thought that Babic had called you, that you had called Stanisic, and Stanisic told me not to go there. But you're right in saying that it was Babic's decision, and it was because of his decision that I didn't go there. But it wasn't Babic who told me that. I was told that by Stanisic. So in my mind, and after what I had read about Babic, that was my interpretation. Now, whether that was so or not, I didn't really I attend any meeting or conversation between you and Babic, but that is my belief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From what you're saying now, could you draw the conclusion, precisely because of the pressure that existed over there, that nobody had really ordered it but simply Jovica Stanisic wanted to protect you from political conflict that had broken out in Krajina at the time between Babic and Martic and the pressure that accompanied those clashes and conflicts?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't think about it along those lines, but there is a certain logic to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you consider it common sense that the political leadership of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Krajina represented by Milan Babic at the time, and you yourself said yesterday that you felt you had been removed from the scene, and then you saw on television Babic saying that Captain Dragan is a mercenary who has been hired to carry out his part of the job, he has been paid out, and he has left. Is that what you said yesterday?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it then clear from that that he wanted to denigrate, minimise what you had done there for the defence of the people of Krajina and at the same time to remove responsibility from himself? Because many people had criticised him, why he had turned against you when, according to some general assessments, you were the most useful man to organise the defence of Krajina, and he was criticized for removing you. And wasn't that a justification he gave, by saying that you were a mercenary and you had -- you had left?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you give me two minutes? I would like to say something, because this has really been bothering me. After the struggle for Glina, the whole situation turned around by 180 degrees. I lived through it. From an absolutely -- absolute impasse on the 4th of April, and the dominant position we had by the 28th of July, this change was such that I had expected, to say the least, a decoration. Instead, I was replaced. I couldn't imagine that I wouldn't get your support and even the support of the JNA and all the political bodies in any possible clash with Babic. So I blamed you, that you hadn't used sufficient authority to bring pressure on Babic. So here you appear to be accused of the opposite. So you can't win either way. I wouldn't like to be in your shoes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But would you allow for the possibility, on the basis of what you quoted from your conversation with Stanisic yesterday, that he wanted to protect you and pull you out of that conflict in Krajina? Because you said yesterday that, walking with you, he said that in Krajina, dirty things were happening, that, unawares, you had become involved in politics there, and that as a result, he believed that -- I didn't hear you use that word, but actually, I think that his intention was to protect you from those pressures and from the position you found yourself in, an unpleasant position because of the dirty things going on there.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible. But if he wanted to protect one man and at the same time allow a defensive system to fall apart that had been established, I found it difficult to accept. But from this point of view today, yes. I think that Stanisic had respect for me for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Judging by what you are saying, you were astonished that upon your return, the fortress had been taken by a disorderly group which did not look like an army, and Frenki came to you, and you say he was upset. He came to that meeting, and he told you that there were problems between Babic and Martic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Let me correct you: He didn't come to the meeting, he came to see me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and then you say that Babic came in after that and that you were rather impolite towards him. You simply considered him to be a negative factor - let me put it that way - for what was going on there.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I considered him to be dishonest, a man who was not of his word. I had been convinced that an agreement had been reached between Martic and Babic, that Martic would lead the armed forces and Babic the political side. And that was stated on one occasion in my presence when both of them were there. And then I realised that Mr. Babic's word meant nothing, that he wanted much more than at the beginning of their relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: His nickname was Titic, if you remember, a small Tito. I asked him about that when he was here, because he wanted to have control of everything, about that nickname, Titic, a small Tito. Tell me, is it true that you told your officers that you were going, and you advised them to ask Frenki about it; that you handed things over to him because he was an intelligence officer, you considered him to be an honourable man, and he would tell them the truth, rather than telling them to follow his command, that he would be their commander. Is my understanding correct or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no doubt that I consider Frenki to be an extremely honourable man to this day. You must understand my position. I hadn't spent a long time in Krajina. I no longer knew who to trust. Frenki, in addition to what you said, was also a Belgrader, and I thought that he would be best informed as to what was going on. So I had a moral duty to address those people. You can't be a commander and then turn your back on those people. I had to say something to them, and I couldn't think of anything better than that, because the decision was taken very quickly. And if anything should happen to me - and I felt that this could happen - so the words I used were, "Listen to what Frenki has to say." It wasn't a command or anything like that. I don't know what Frenki would have done with such an order from me anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us move on. Since you are mentioning Babic and his political activities and ambitions in the area of Krajina, would you agree that this was a man who opted for peace or was it a man who wanted to control the army and whose option was that of war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I shall try to leave out my emotions, because I really have many reasons not to like this man. This was a man who got up at 2.00 or 3.00 in the afternoon. He never arrived at the office before then. Secondly, he had a quarrel with me as to why I wouldn't allow beards and a Chetnik image among the Knindza.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So criticised you for not allowing beards and a Chetnik image among the Knindza; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In that period, he was very close to Seselj, and I think he liked that option. You heard of the incident that occurred later with the busload of Seselj's men, so that, in my opinion, he even criticised the Z-4 plan, that he said, "We will never allow Belgrade to bring pressure on us, that Belgrade wants to make a gift of a part of the Krajina territory," and he was a major opponent to the signing of the Vance Plan and the disarmament, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have a particular conflict with Babic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, I grew up - and you probably noticed that while you were in power - I have a certain attitude towards politicians in power. In fact, that is my political option, to always be in the opposition. I was in the opposition during Tito's days, during your day, and even nowadays, and that is my option. So I never had any close relations with him. So I thought, what have I got to talk to him about? So we had very little contact except when we had to, and then I just respected his position, just as I respected you if -- I don't know whether you remember: We met at the entrance to the Military Medical Academy and I greeted you courteously, as I did during this ceremony courteously, but my private opinion of politicians in power is always a negative one. I always look for their negative sides, in that way feeling that I will encourage them to do better.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about Babic's activities with respect to the arming or formation of a unit down there outside of the structures that had legally been established in Krajina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very little, except that I snatched away from him two cisterns, two tanks, two fuel tanks containing weapons. When I say snatched it from him, the secret service had informed me that the border was being crossed -- it would be crossed. When I'm talking about the border, I'm talking about the Grahovo border between Bosnia, that two trucks would cross the border carrying weapons that were not intended for me. To tell you the truth, we in Krajina had so many weapons that more weapons went from Krajina to Belgrade than vice versa. The weapons coming from Serbia were hunting weapons reaching us through private channels, at least, as far as I know. So I intercepted those trucks. I could maybe even find the name of the driver. When I asked him, "Where are you talking these weapons?" He said, "They are for Babic." We seized those weapons, and as the man was coming with the best intentions, we released the driver and we kept those weapons, expecting Babic to react. There was no particular reaction towards me, but as far as I can remember, Frenki informed me later, though what I'm going to say needs to be checked. I think Frenki said that he complained either to you or to someone else that we were stealing weapons from him. But I don't know the details. Anyway, this didn't reach me. There were Thompsons, 45 among those weapons, conserved weapons from the Second World War which had been kept stored away somewhere in a state of conservation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But you explained that Babic's -- Babic was the main political figure and that Martic headed the defence.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then for whom was Babic procuring those weapons?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For some Chetniks of his who later on, as far as I know, looted Drnis. I wasn't there, but that was the information that reached me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's quite sufficient, Captain, thank you. Is it true that a large number of members of your unit, after the takeover of power by Babic in Krajina and the conflict with Martic when he pushed Martic back, that some of the members of units were out of favour and that they left the Krajina and went to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 4, paragraph 3, you refer to this. You say that a part of your unit went to a training camp in Fruska Gora.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was at my initiative. And the authority I had with Frenki, when I said to him that I had the moral obligation towards these men who were under me, who trusted me and who were now out of work and who Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. had some knowledge that could be of use to the service because, after all, there was a war going on, that he should admit them to the service. And he promised that he would do as much as he could in view of the position he held at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that this Fruska Gora camp was a kind of isolation for those men so that they could be under control while they were in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A kind of reception centre. It would be better for them to be kept in one place than for them to disperse all over the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that most of them, when they wanted to return to the areas from which they had come, left on their own initiative and joined the commands of the towns they had come from or wherever they thought they could be of assistance in the defence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To gain a proper perspective - and I have a feeling that the Tribunal may think that this was some sort of an army - we're talking about 15 to 25 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm talking of a small group of men.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some returned immediately, saying, "What are we doing here, sitting around while a war is being waged?" And some others were waiting to return when the conditions were ready for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Captain, quite briefly, how did your unit or the popular Knindza get weapons in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were already weapons in Krajina. Do not forget that I arrived there on the 4th of April. And there had been many battles by then. I didn't arrive there before the beginning of the conflict. I arrived there a year after the beginning of the conflict. So there were weapons there already. And I think it was a Colonel Dragisic, who was the commander of the Territorial Defence, who had the keys to the TO warehouse. Later on, we stole a little from the army. I brought the first armoured vehicles from Glina, the first anti-tank rockets. I got them from the Ustashas. Later on, what UNPROFOR had left to the Croats and when we took over that territory again, we took some of the UNPROFOR weaponry. So we could have captured much more weapons than we were able to use, so that the weapons were not a major problem. A much greater problem were the weapons coming from Krajina to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that, apart from a small calibre gun, you did not have any heavy weapons in your unit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a 14-millimetre cannon from the Second World War that one Serb had kept and kept it in readiness. We should all ask ourselves why, over 50 years in Tito's time of brotherhood and unity, someone felt it necessary to keep a gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Buried somewhere, conserved.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, kept in combat readiness, regularly lubricated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 6, paragraph 8, you say that your unit was already very famous by 1991 and that Serbs from all corners of the country assisted you, brought aid, equipment, that that never was a problem. They even brought you many things that were of absolutely no use to you, but what really mattered was the great goodwill to help you, and what was useful and what wasn't was a different matter. Is that the proper description of the atmosphere and attitude to your unit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's exactly the way it was. It was an all people's movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that as far as financing is concerned, it went through Martic. So I'm asking you, was it normal and logical for Martic, as the first man in the police, to be the best informed and the most competent in the distribution of resources, equipment, and assistance in general received by the Serbian army of Krajina and the Serbian police, including aid from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. That was the only proper way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there a single piece of heavy or small weapon that you received in Krajina from a member of the security service in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only piece of weaponry was the CZ-99 pistol I received from Jovica Stanisic as his own personal gift to me with an inscription and a card, and I believed he made it to me man to man. That is the only piece of weaponry received, and not a single shot was fired from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is how we do it in our country; a gift as a sign of respect and friendship, as a token of his respect for you, with an inscription. That was nothing unusual?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, are you going to refer to the statements continuously? Would you like the Judges to have the statement? Please bear in mind the Judges don't have the statements, unless you ask us to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't need to ask for it because I have no dispute with the witness over authenticity. So there is no need for me to prove to you that he is not telling the truth. Whenever I quote him, he says that is indeed what he said, and I think that is sufficient. Thank you very much for your good intentions, Mr. Kwon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only wish, and you will decide yourselves whether you need it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution wouldn't object to the Chamber -- if Mr. Milosevic wants to admit the statement. The Prosecution may very well do it on re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 392.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It doesn't quite fit, and I'm referring to something that I read in your statement, it doesn't quite fit with your testimony, so I want us to clear this matter up. I will ask you a couple of questions, and then we will try to put your answers together one by one to get the best possible reflection of reality. On page 4 of your statement, in line 1, you say: "In my opinion, the war effort was financed by the Serbian government, but I have no proof of that."

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who says that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says so in your statement on page 4. Will you please look at it. I would really like us to clarify this. That is your statement of the 23rd, 24th, 26th August. I'm talking about the statement in B/C/S. I don't know where it is in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's the -- page 4. It's the second paragraph. I might note that since Mr. Vasiljkovic speaks English, the statement was given in English, I would suggest that perhaps the best copy for the witness to work from is the language in which he made the statement, which would be the English copy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember saying this at all. Maybe it was taken out of context. I can't place it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it's not something that you could testify to, that the war effort --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's absolutely no logic to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Because I was listening to your testimony, and what is written here makes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a minute. It's in the middle of page 4.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] I'm sorry. In the middle?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Could you find: "We wore green camouflage combat uniforms." Three lines from there. "In my opinion, Serbian government financed the war effort. However, I have no evidence."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I might have -- [Interpretation] I may have made a comment to the effect that Krajina or -- I don't remember my precise answer, because I only have answers here, not the questions. It depends on what the question was. Maybe the question was whether financial assistance was being sent to Krajina during the war. So my answer would have been yes, and it's normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Of course it is. But I don't think it can be treated as the financing of some sort of war effort, because that's precisely the point. It is put in a context here that absolutely distorts reality.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly does. I don't know how this found its way into my statement, although I see my initials on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Captain, you are not the first witness here who finds in his statement things he hadn't meant to say.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I wish to tell you this: In addition to those questions which are always open, such as my opposition to your use of the 92 bis article, the use of statements in which we don't see the questions asked is very dubious from the point of view of establishing the truth, so that testifying on the basis of written statements with only cross-examination allowed is also very dubious, because completely different answers can be given to various questions, and taken out of context, they create a completely different, untruthful picture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The answer is this, that we do not have a tape recording - and I don't know of any system that does - usually of the questions and answers. What we have are the statements which are taken down as a result. The protection, as far as the truth is concerned, is to be found, or should be found in the fact that each page has the witness's signature on it, that at the beginning, the witness says that the information is true "to the best of my knowledge and belief," and that at the end, in the standard form, the witness acknowledges, signs that the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. statement has been read over to him, he's given it voluntarily, and that he may be called to give evidence. So those are such protections as the Court has. Now, we have to make do with the statements as we have them. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And one thing you should do is that you have to put the full text to the witness. The phrase which has been referred to is related to the uniform. "A local company had made the uniforms for us. All the funding came from Martic Milan. In my opinion, Serbian government financed the war efforts."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not use the term "war effort" for sure. This is not my word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry that I signed it. I don't know how that went past. Okay, if I might describe it, I reject it. This is not my terminology. I don't know how that came through. It could have been a genuine mistake. I don't think -- I don't believe that people that worked with me would go into the trouble of doing -- I think it's just a misunderstanding. At the end, I don't think, even if I said that, my opinion, based on nothing, would -- should count in any way anyway. I'm not a -- you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I think the point has been made in relation to this, and no need to take any further time on it. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So would it be fair to say that material assistance extended by Serbia to the people in Krajina who were in danger, this material assistance is treated in this explanation here as the financing of the war effort?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Whereas it was not the financing of the war effort. It was material assistance to the jeopardised people in Krajina? Is that what material assistance means?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, and it was insufficient, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was as large as we could afford. In any case, material assistance is one thing and the financing of the war effort is another thing. Now, let's see another answer. I will, I will. Don't you worry. You remember that it was precisely Serbia and me personally who insisted on the acceptance of the Vance-Owen plan and that this issue gave rise to my open conflict with the then leader of Krajina, Milan Babic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My influence could only have been political in nature, and do you remember that I sent open letter in which I stated my views on his detrimental activity to the people of Krajina? You know that he refused to sign this plan?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And he continued on insisting on the war option?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He wouldn't accept the Vance Plan, and on that score even your influence did not help. It was distorted because he held himself out who -- as a man who refused to surrender Krajina and you as the person who wanted to sell out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And even based on facts, we can see from here that we sent our assistance to the people who were in danger and who needed to defend themselves. But the very fact that we insisted on the peaceful solution speaks in support of my claim that it was not financing of the war effort but material assistance to the people in danger.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you didn't see it as financing of your activities?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is certain that money did not come into my pockets while I was there, from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us conclude this part. Captain, talking about the Republic of Serbian Krajina, can we talk at all about armed Serbian people who were fighting for their own lives, for their families, for their homeland in an area which they had populated for centuries rather than an aggression on the part of those people or on the part of Serbia who supported them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely agree with you that it is the only possible understanding or definition of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in your experience, those people were very much afraid for their lives and existence, in view of the circumstances we already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is absolutely no doubt about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Captain, do you know anything at all from any source about some plan for the creation of a Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even from this film that we saw, and let us remind ourselves that it is a secret film from the Serbian secret service in which the presidents of Serbia arrived. It was not the Serbian hymn that we saw, that played; it was the Yugoslav hymn. It was never felt that anyone in Serbia, except jokingly, tongue in cheek, was talking about Greater Serbia. It was entirely propaganda, enemy propaganda. And it was so ridiculous that this poor country of Serbia, so impoverished, on its knees with all these members of the secret service, and you saw them in the film, there was not a single boss among them, should be talking about the creation of some great Serbian state. It was pure nonsense, and only somebody with the most ill intentions could present it as something serious.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is what the opposite side is saying. I completely agree with you, Captain. It is only the way to interpret it. Let's move on. Is it true that after the attack of Croatian armed forces on Serbian Krajina on the 20th of January, 1993, it was in Milovica, the Miljevina plateau, you decided to return to Krajina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an across-the-board appeal from the government of Krajina regardless of the fact that Jovica Stanisic advised me, banned me from going there. I decided to go there nevertheless because it seemed silly to me to walk the streets of Belgrade and have people ask me in the street, "What are you doing here, Captain, while people are being killed in Krajina?" I simply couldn't stay in Belgrade. I returned to Krajina. And I returned accompanied by one single man and one journalist of the Nin magazine. The three of us went there. So I didn't go there with a unit representing Serbia. We were three men in one car. We went down there and we put ourselves at the disposal of the then government of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about the events preceding the incursion into the Miljevina plateau?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had so much to think about, so many problems with the wounded, thousands of them coming from all battlefields, that I read the press and followed the media very superficially, and I'm really not competent to comment on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you know that according to the Vance-Owen Plan, the Serbs put all their weapons under the control of the United Nations, under lock.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You know that the Serbian forces attacked the Miljevac plateau which was in a UN protected area. They recaptured their weapons, seeing that the UNPROFOR does not wish or cannot protect them. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. And I know one more thing: There was a belief in Krajina that Yugoslavia was the guarantor of the cease-fire between Serbs and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So under those circumstances, you decided to go back, since the agreement was not being observed, there was an attack, people were again in danger. They recaptured the weapons that they had turned over, in accordance with the plan.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And seeing that, you say that you decided to go back to Krajina to help the cause. That's what you said on page 9, paragraph 2. Tell me, what do you understand under the term "cause"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please don't hold my terminology against me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not holding anything against you. Just tell me, what do you imply?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I imply defence against an enemy who does not respect the cease-fire or the rules of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you then approached Goran Hadzic, and he told you to go and see General Mile Novakovic who was then commander of the headquarters of the Serbian army of Krajina, the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that during your stay during in the Republic of Serbian Krajina in 1993, 1994, and 1995, you actually were an officer of the army of Serbian Krajina and your job was to conduct the training of the troops as an instructor and training advisor?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that you were appointed to that post by an order of the then commander of the army of Serbian Krajina, the General Novakovic I just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone from Serbia send you there to go back to Krajina after the attack on the Miljevac plateau?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In that period, I almost had no contact with the service at all due to a conflict which I described yesterday. And I did not wish to contact Frenki either lest I brought him into a position where he would have to choose between his service and our friendship.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it indisputable that it was only your reputation and popularity Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. among the people in Krajina that made the commander in the Krajina appoint you to the post which meant you were in charge of the training of troops in Bruska?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I suppose at that time you had many contacts and frequent contacts with many officers of the army of Serbian Krajina. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it well known -- and please think about this carefully before you answer. You met with many of them, talked to them. Did any of them receive an order to leave the army of Yugoslavia and go to the Republic of Serbian Krajina? Was it an order given to any one of them who used to be officers of the JNA? Was a single one of them ordered to leave the JNA and go to the army of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't meet anyone who did, and I didn't meet there anyone who wasn't a native of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. While we are talking about this, can we agree that it is correct that the greatest majority of them came of their own free will, feeling it as their own patriotic duty, whereas a part of them had responded to the appeal issued to the effect that those who were born there should go and help out?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm certain that many of them arrived there with the same motivation that I shared. One thing is certain: I can't remember anyone who wasn't a native of the area, and I had met hundreds of officers. I can say 100 per cent, or let's make it 95 per cent of them were natives the area. I don't remember meeting a single Belgrader.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can it be said that the JNA exerted pressure on people from Krajina and that they were told they had to go back to Krajina? Did you meet a single officer from Krajina who intimated to you in any way that he had gone back under pressure from a command in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the contrary. There were cases when certain officers who had arrived were not well accepted by the environment because they were accused of being communist officers. They had come of their own free will, and I don't remember that any of them had been subjected to any sort of proceedings. If you give me a chance to answer at least one part of what he said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to stop this now. It's time for an adjournment. We will resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Captain, the previous witness, General Vasiljevic, mentioned you here as Martic's mercenary and as an exponent of the State Security Service of Serbia. Do you believe that there are any grounds for either of these allegations that he made here?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I have given a lot of my time to this Tribunal, so please give me a little time to respond, because this is the only witness statement that has really scared me. When talking about Mr. Vasiljevic, we're talking about the head of the counter-intelligence service of the army, a man with fantastic resources at his disposal to reveal the facts, and I was seriously concerned by hearing such a statement. As far as I remember, he said that it took quite a lot of time for them to learn that the service had brought me from Australia to Krajina. I think we have to take his statement seriously, and I'm sure the Tribunal does so, but it is such nonsense. In 1983, I left Australia, and this is something that can easily be verified. I spent three years cruising on my yacht in the Indian Ocean. I came here from Africa. Now, why did this cause concern? It is because somebody who should have known everything was unable to discover basic facts about a man who is moving around with weapons in his own territory. He can't say that this didn't interest him and he could have very simply found out. So he's either lying or he's absolutely incapable. I don't believe that he's lying, so I think he's just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not going to stop you for a moment, but there must come an end to this. As you appreciate, you're a witness here, not to argue a case either way, and what we depend on is your answers to questions which are factual. Now, at the moment you're arguing a case against what it's alleged somebody else said. I don't recollect precisely that piece of evidence, but we will not stop now on that point. But we hear what you say. You deny that that's true, and no doubt we'll hear argument about it in due course. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So his statement that the state security service had brought you from Australia is not true?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You didn't even come from Australia to Krajina. You came from the United States, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time from Africa, the second time from the United States, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Rrahim Ademi is? Have you heard of his name?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is an officer in the Croatian army, isn't he, who later went somewhere? Do you mean him? That's what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that he's an Albanian, a member of the Croatian army who participated in the massacre of Serbs in the Medak pocket? Do you remember that? Had you heard of that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had arrived there with my men after that massacre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you hear, and according to your information, is that the same man who later, as a member of the terrorist KLA, carried out a series of crimes in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, wait a minute. Do you know any of this from your own knowledge as opposed to something you may have read about or something of that sort? I thought your evidence was limited to the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with you. I cannot tell you much about Kosovo or Bosnia, only what I read from the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. I won't ask you anything about Kosovo. But do you know how many Albanians from Kosovo took part on the Croatian side during the fighting for Gospic, for instance, the battles for Gospic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the battle was ongoing for Gospic, I was in Belgrade. I didn't take part in that battle, but I was informed by people who were in contact with me that there were quite a number of Albanians who voluntarily went to fight on the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know, but not only from the media, that if not all, then most of them afterwards, as members of the terrorist KLA, were the actual perpetrators of crimes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to stop this. The witness has said he can't deal with Kosovo. Now, you're not to put to him tendentious matters which you no doubt are going to rely on. You must call evidence about it. There's no point asking him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I have to ask him a question from the point of view of motivation, shall I call it that, for his engagement that I have already asked him about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, tell me, please, Captain, why the participation of Serbs from Krajina in the Serbian army of Krajina in the war for the defence of the Serbian people would be a crime and an evil act, whereas the participation of Albanians in the Croatian army and in massacres --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is a pure comment, not a question. Now, your time is limited, as you know, so you should make the best use of it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, as far as my time is concerned, tomorrow after the first break I have another one hour and 15 minutes, because the witness testified all day yesterday and for an hour and 15 minutes today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will decide on that in due course, but let's move on now with this witness. We shall be adjourning the evidence at half past one, to deal with administrative matters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you this question in connection with Krajina, but I will repeat the same question linked to your knowledge regarding Bosnia, since on page 11, second paragraph, you said that you didn't believe that a single unit or so-called paramilitary unit could have acted in Krajina without the permission of the army, the police, and the state security. Is it clear that in that case you are referring to the army, police, and state security of the Serbian Krajina and Republika Srpska and not to the state security of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. I never refer to the police, state security or the army of the Republic of Serbia. I don't think that anyone in Serbia today can have an army without the permission of the army, the police, or the state security of Serbia, which is quite normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 10, in paragraph 2, you mention you're going to Bosnia and your involvement with the release of a Muslim sportsman. I think he was a rower, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, you clashed with a certain Pavlovic who headed the Territorial Defence down there, and from what is contained in your statement, you assumed that he was a member of the Serbian state security. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Are you referring to the state security of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In that case, I meant the state security of Serbia. And later on, when I checked this out - and I told the investigators this too - I learnt much more about this gentleman. He's an ordinary cheat, a freak, who one day would say he was a member of the state security, a friend of Captain Dragan, a friend of Patriarch Paul. So that was my opinion at the time. As I was in conflict with the service of the time, in my mind this seemed to fit. But I told the investigators that I later on learnt that he had no connection with the Serbian state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I just wanted to establish that. There is no dispute also that in the past you were my political opponent and that frequently you did not agree with my political views. So tell me now, do you believe that I or anyone else from Serbia had in any way prepared, organised, aided and abetted in the commission of any crime in Krajina throughout your stay there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not the witness's belief which is evidence. If you want to ask him the question in this way, you can: Do you know -- wait a minute. Do you know -- his belief is irrelevant. What isn't irrelevant is any state of knowledge he has, and if you want, you can ask him does he know of any crime which you committed, if you want, or your connection with any crime. If you want to ask that question, you can, but you want to ask him in that form.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You heard my question, Captain. So do you consider -- I will replace that with the words do you have any direct or indirect knowledge about that, that I or anyone else from Serbia had prepared, organised, instigated, or committed a crime in the territory of Krajina while you were there? Do you have any direct or indirect knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As your political opponent, that is something I never concealed. If I had had any such knowledge, I think I would have done everything to make that public so that you would be dismissed from the position you held, so that never for a moment did I have any information or knowledge or even belief that you or any other member of the Serbian system had ordered or participated or had knowledge about any crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Captain, tell me, as an experienced man for these military matters in connection with certain crimes which certainly did happen in the territory of Serbian Krajina - there's no doubt about that - can you claim that any of that was the result of anybody's orders or policies, or was it something that attends any such conflict and which was always an individual act on the part of an individual or a group that committed it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of my experience in Krajina, and not only experience but during my 12 years of work with the victims of war, I think I can provide a precise explanation which may assist the Tribunal which, after all, Their Honours were not on the spot, so we can clarify some things in connection with crimes. It is virtually impossible -- that is my belief: It is impossible to send an order to commit a crime from the top because along the chain of command, there must be a normal man who will not do that. It is far more probable for a crime to be committed at the bottom, and in the chain of command for somebody to be found who will cover it up. Why? Because the first person witnessed it, and when he reported about it, he belittled it, and as it goes up the chain of command, it becomes of lesser and lesser magnitude. So I don't know if I have made myself clear. If we wish to capture a war criminal, it is far better to start from the victim than from the top and point your finger in a vacuum.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can we conclude that what was happening is characteristic of that type of a conflict such as the civil war in Yugoslavia was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a theory that I firmly believe in. When an armed people goes to war, they do so with emotions, and those emotions are fear and hatred, and hatred is most frequently produced by fear, and everyone who's studied psychology will know that. So we had precisely such a situation when football fans set the war in motion. Imagine a match that we all watched and went wrong, and imagine if those fans had weapons. You see what they do even when they are unarmed. And that is precisely the sort of thing that happened there, that deep-felt fear, and also the fear on the other side, the fear of Chetniks produced by Bulajic's films created such hatred among unprofessional users of weapons, people who were -- who put on a uniform and were told, "From now on, you're a soldier." Do not forget that the power of weapons, even basic weapons nowadays, are tenfold what they were during the Second World War. So that I believe tomorrow if a war were to break out between the Netherlands and the neighbouring countries - God forbid - and if the citizens were to be armed and go to war, I think there -- the situation would be similar and there would be even more crimes than there were over there. And please do not forget that I am probably one of the officers who arrested most of his own men for the purpose of prevention or for violations of any code of war -- warfare.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You know that Satish Nambiar, the commander of UNPROFOR, said words to that effect too. He said he'd never received any report from his subordinates from genocide but that these are conflicts typical of that type of conflict anywhere in the world and developments and events that are typical. Did you hear Satish Nambiar perhaps?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I hear this for the first time. I'm sorry not to have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you give me a direct answer to this question: Do you know that anyone, let us leave aside Serbia but even in Krajina, that the authorities in Krajina, starting from Milan Martic who headed the police and the defence forces for most of the time, that anyone was given orders to commit a crime?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have no such information, nor do I believe that anyone would have the courage to do any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you now to deny or confirm something that Martic told me in those days, since you were a close associate of his for a time in Krajina. He said to me that the rights of the Croats in Krajina, those who remained living there, were fully protected and that in no way were the Croats discriminated against as compared to the Serbian population living in Krajina. Is that your own experience or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had very few contacts, which is quite understandable, with Croatian civilians. Simply I avoided it, because I believed that a Croat in Krajina would not be too happy seeing a Serb in uniform close to him. So I did my best to make a detour around the places inhabited by Croats. I had a couple of cases when, in my area of responsibility, there were Croatian families, and exceptional measures were taken to protect those families, to feed them, to provide medical care for them. And I am quite certain that the investigators must have in their possession documents confirming such a situation, documents from the UNPROFOR forces who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There is no doubt that they are aware of the truth, but there's a difference between what they know and what is presented here. So can I draw the conclusion from what you said that this coincides practically with what Martic told me, that care was taken of them, good care was taken of them, and there was no discrimination. The authorities tried, in relation to possible irresponsible acts on the part of civilians or a member of the armed forces of the Krajina, to protect every Croat in that area from that.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You just said what I wanted to mention myself. There were certain incidents. I remember in November when I went there for a couple of days, I saw in prison a Serb who was suspected of having committed a crime. He was imprisoned. It was in November. And I don't believe that despite individual incidents it could have been a general policy of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was it exactly the opposite? Was it the policy of the authorities of Krajina, that anyone who committed a crime must be prosecuted and turned over to the authorities, to the judiciary?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the way I understood it. And in my zone of responsibility, and even outside it sometimes, I acted on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: According to what you say in response to my questions, it transpires that Martic was telling the truth to me. Do you consider him to be an honourable man and a patriot?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. I believe him to be a man of honour and a man of his word.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us move on. On page 4, paragraph 4, of your second statement, you say that Dafina Milanovic, the banker, after your withdrawal supposedly from Krajina, expressed her desire to help you, and you mentioned even during your examination-in-chief that she placed at your disposal 1 million Deutschmarks which you didn't take for yourself but placed them in a fund used for the supply of equipment to Krajina, including kevlar vests, all sorts of military equipment. When was that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That happened when the decision was made to establish this centre in Fruska Gora to collect these young men who were leaving Krajina after my replacement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, the fact that she helped you and that she wanted to give you some financial assistance even, did it seem to you that she was doing so under some sort of pressure from the government or because she simply wanted, as a patriot, to help the cause of Serbian defence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She certainly didn't do it under pressure from the government, but I said to Frenki that I procured uniforms. He was happy as a puppy. It was certainly not her motive -- it was certainly her motive to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. wish to help the defence. And because of my popularity at the time, she also may have seen it as serving her commercial interests to be seen as somebody assisting this popular captain. So you have there two different motives which may have been behind this act. But the purchase of this equipment and this aid that I gave for that purpose was my own initiative and my own way of joining the defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I will not ask you more questions about this because you talked at great length about battles for Glina. I just want to clarify one detail. If I noted it down correctly yesterday, you said that, to the members in the fighting over there -- there were not many of you. Twenty, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, about 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: To those people, you wanted to make some sort of gift, and you had nothing to give them but red berets. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Those were called at the time the Red Berets of Krajina; is that so?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that have anything to do with the unit for special operations of Serbia or the Special Operations Unit of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in a very special way that I will have to explain. The people who created the JSO, in other words Frenki Simatovic, he needed a tradition to put behind a unit that did not exist. And later, some of these young men from this area whom he took under his wing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let him finish.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, since --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would you like to finish what you were going to say? Don't interrupt all the time. Let him give his account.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He simply started appropriating traditions. He asked me if I had any souvenirs from battles in Glina, from Ljubovo, and I gave him what I had. He was driven by the desire to lend importance and tradition to a unit which never exceeded a company in strength. It must have created a great impression on you, Mr. President, to see those men lined up and to see that armband on them, but to anyone who knows anything about military matters, it is clear that it was a small unit, and to give it more authority, Frenki needed some sort of biography. And Frenki started building up that history, that biography for the unit, in the best of intentions, to create a positive effect, a positive image. That's why you saw those maps of Glina, those weapons captured from - what's his name? I'm getting on age, it seems. That famous Ustasha and so on and so forth. Just as here in the Tribunal you see some souvenirs from Krajina on the walls, it's the same thing that existed there. That is the only link in the technical sense. This was used for propaganda, to promote the image of the unit. I don't see anything wrong with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't see anything wrong with it either, and we will come back to that later when we see that film.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And don't you worry, Mr. May, I'm not going to try to restrict the witness in his testimony because I don't see that he has anything to hide. I believe you should apply the same practice to the opposite side when they tell the witness to answer their questions only with a yes or no or when they interrupt him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If they are doing anything wrong, they will be stopped. But they do it in order to speed things up. So perhaps you might do the same.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's precisely what I'm doing. But this, "Let the witness answer," has already become a tradition whenever I interrupt the witness, and it applies exclusively to cross-examination, never in chief. But let us move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So from the viewpoint of this fact, and we'll come back to that later, the fact that certain fighters in the area of Krajina, Republika Srpska, later joined the Special Operations Unit which was established much later within the state security department of Serbia, the tradition belonged to individuals that belonged to such units, not to the unit itself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. And just as we have today in the Tribunal former observers from Krajina. There is no other link.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to just one detail from your description of the fighting around Glina. I wrote down here, "An officer of the JNA --"

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
