utterances.text: Boric or Drobnjak. Grujica Boric.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: After a single shell fired, he ordered to -- through a megaphone that the JNA cease fire because Chetniks and units -- Ustashas are fighting. The JNA has nothing to do with it. The JNA was playing a buffer between those forces. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that on your way back, when you were all exhausted after the takeover of Glina, you heard, although it was outside your zone of responsibility, you heard along the way, in a place called Strugar, that some people had committed a crime. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you went there, arrested those people, and put them in prison.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a crime against Croats. Let me be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, against Croats. Who were those people who committed that crime against Croats? Were they civilians or were they members of some sort of armed formations of the Serbian army of Krajina or the TO or the police or anyone else?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, but please bear in mind that we hadn't slept for five days, we spent one day clearing the mines, at that time I had 20 kilos less than today, I seem to remember the information we got was this: Those people had committed a crime, and I believe I did all that can be expected from a very exhausted man, and bear in mind I hadn't seen the corpses, I hadn't been to Strugar, I hadn't visited the hospital, but the assessment was that the person informing me about it was telling the truth. I detained those people, locked them up, and since I didn't trust anyone with the key, I kept the key until Martic showed up. Then I gave the key to Martic and went to sleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many were the people you arrested?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were 16, and they were between 10 and 12. I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it was a group of TO members, local TO members.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what happened with them later?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I inquired. Somebody told me that the military security took them over from Martic, but this has to be checked out. I really don't know. Soon after that, I went to Belgrade, so that the entire incident became history to me. And I asked people in Krajina later if any trial followed after that, and they didn't know. So this was simply superseded by more important, more recent events. And I don't remember whether Frenki asked me to write to him something about it. It was one of the very few reports which I actually put in writing, but it was more on a friend-to-friend basis than anything formal. It was for the sake of our personal relationship, not through official channels.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In any case, at the time you were a member of the Krajina police, and having learned of potential perpetrators of potential crime against the Croats, so you arrested them, and the rest was not your job.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. I was not competent to conduct an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us go back to those red berets. So you distributed to them those red berets and those were red berets of Krajina, not of a special operations unit from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You talked today, and I noted it down, in Skelani some man called Pupovac set up a unit of Red Berets, and then you mentioned Teslic where some sort of company was formed, but it was municipal Red Berets, not Red Berets as part of the army of Republika Srpska. Then again in Brcko, there were Red Berets of the SAO of Semberija and Majevica; right? That's what was mentioned this morning. Is it true that after these distributions of red berets to this small group of ten people it became very popular and was copied in many municipalities of Serbian Krajina and elsewhere? Many small detachments were formed called Red Berets. You mentioned Skelani, Teslic, Brcko. I don't know if there were any other cases, but you must know many more. In many places it became a fashion almost.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even in Yugoslavia, the 63rd Assault Brigade adopted the name Red Berets. It was considered as something that could attract young people. It became a general fashion. Everybody wanted to become a member of the Red Berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's all I wanted to hear from you, because your predecessor Vasiljevic claimed that all these Red Berets were members of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia or even the special units of the MUP of Serbia. Let us move on to our next topic, Captain. You took part in the fighting around Skabrnja; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In this fighting, did you participate as a member of the army of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. But please, before we finish with Skabrnja, give me one minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead. That's precisely what I wanted to ask you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Skabrnja is very frequently mentioned, because allegedly - and I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. wasn't there at the time, I must say - in 1991, sometime in December, Skabrnja, as we know, is a Croatian village where units under the command of the JNA committed some crime. I had nothing to do with it because I wasn't there. In 1993, the UNPROFOR was stationed there, the French UNPROFOR who was supposed to hold the demarcation line between Serbs and Croats. They withdrew and the Croats retook Skabrnja and certain other positions as well. I came down there, and that is the only area, the only territory which we managed to liberate again and even move a little forward to reach the positions we held previously. I had very little forces in 1993 when there was the attack on the Miljevac plateau. I just want to make one thing clear. Captain Dragan has nothing to do with Skabrnja 1991 and has everything to do with Skabrnja 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you have nothing to do with Skabrnja 1991, and you have everything to do with the events in 1993.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Would I be right in saying, based on the information I got, that at that time, at the time of that fighting, there were no Croat civilians in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was not a single civilian. There hadn't been any civilians in Skabrnja for two years by then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the strength of the Croatian force in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My information was that they had one brigade in position. I believe it was the 115th Brigade. I'm not sure. But a lot was written about it, so it's not difficult to check. It was quite a large force deployed in that area between Zadar and Beograd.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You took part there as a member of the Serbian army of Krajina. Therefore, you accomplished that assignment in accordance with the plan which was to secure that defence line of Krajina that had been jeopardised by Croatian forces despite the presence of the UNPROFOR; is that so?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that at your invitation a unit of Arkan's volunteers came to assist you and on that occasion suffered major losses? That's the information I have. Is this piece of information true or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I had under my command only two platoons, that is about 60 men, at one point I was in half encirclement, and I sent out an appeal for help, and then a unit arrived to assist me, a unit that had been in the vicinity on my right flank. That unit of volunteers was commanded by Legija. They came to my help and, during that operation, suffered major losses. I believe there was seven killed or something like that. At Martic's request, they left Krajina couple of days later, a couple of days after they helped me out. And we took over Krajina -- sorry. We took over Skabrnja 14 days after they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, please, as briefly as you can, do you believe that they acted in a soldierly manner, courageously? Did they fight as soldiers or were they committing crimes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all my encounters on the battlefield with them, they observed the soldiers' code of honour. Of course I don't know everything about them, but from what I saw, they acted in a manner which deserves every praise, and I'm very grateful to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Certain things are ascribed to them which were not corroborated by any facts or documents. This is why I'm asking. You say that they fought courageously, but did they fight honourably?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that case where I was present, they deserve every praise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm only asking you, Captain, about things you can testify to. I'm not asking you to talk about things you know nothing about or did not witness. And why did Martic insist that they leave Krajina? Was there a clash with them or among them or were there some political or other reasons involved? Do you know of any reason at all?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will be telling you my own opinion now because I was not present during that conflict, but I think my opinion will do. There was some personal hostility between Zeljko Raznjatovic and Martic, and Martic simply didn't want to tolerate under him anyone who did not treat him with sufficient respect that Martic expected to enjoy. So I think it's a matter of personal conflict between Raznjatovic and Martic rather than any other reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So we are now in the area of vanity rather than any events or objective reasons.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you will agree with me that vanity ranks very high in our Serbian minds. Sometimes it supersedes even the national interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in the case of Milan Babic, I believe it became very clear. I don't know whether you share my opinion.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You answered, let me say, certain questions with lengthy explanations, and I want to use my time rationally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Milosevic, it's nearly half past. That might be a convenient moment to stop. You'll have two hours -- you will have two hours tomorrow, if you want it. Up to two hours tomorrow. You don't have to spend that time with the witness. Mr. Vasiljkovic, that's all for today. Could you be back, please, at 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, before we begin, let me deal with just one or two matters by way of a programme so we can deal with them, particularly the 92 bis statements, in a fairly orderly and rational way. We'll deal with General Mangan today, plus the point about the pseudonyms if you've got a report ready now. Tomorrow we will find time to deal with those three witnesses who I identified to whom the amici took specific objection, and that was B-1732, C-1201, C-1231. Next week we will go on with the Vukovar statements, so far as I've identified them, and I will give the numbers so that preparation can be made: C-006, C-1149, C-1164 and 5, C-1126, C-1071, and C-1171. At a convenient moment next week we'll address those and any other connected Vukovar statements anyone can identify.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff can deal with General Mangan now. She can also confirm to you -- I think. She can also confirm to you that she has made a filing in respect of the three witnesses you want dealt with tomorrow, to save time.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, as my colleague just said, we have prepared a filing that will reach you today in relation to these three persons, and I think that will deal with the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in relation to General Mangan, I have already mentioned yesterday that we have a similar case like in the case of Mr. Davies, that we had proposed to hear General Mangan live on all matters that are actually here in dispute; that means the defence of Dubrovnik, the conduct of artillery operations, and the reasoning behind the attack on Dubrovnik. And the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: For the rest, he was a European Monitor, and he deals with his deployment. He was in Croatia for a short time, and most of the evidence, in fact, will have to be given live, in any event, because according to my notes, it will be simplest if paragraphs 12, 17 to 27, and 33 be given live. Yes. Thank you. Anything, Mr. Kay, on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There is the additional issue, I believe, with this witness - I'm just turning it up - of dealings with Milan Babic, part of the joint criminal enterprise. There's an issue we raised in our filing on the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can we --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm looking at page 3 of the English. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do we need that to be given live? It doesn't seem very controversial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's not necessary perhaps live but it's certainly an issue that I should imagine the accused will be looking at when I'm looking at the central passage. He was clearly in control of the state of affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that would be in evidence, and if the accused wants to cross-examine about it, of course he can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic, apart from your standard objection, the -- what will happen is that this evidence would be admitted, it's proposed under Rule 92 bis, but the majority would have been given live, including the paragraphs which I have mentioned. Anything you want to say about that? You will have the opportunity to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's exclusively a matter regarding the cross-examination that is important. In addition to the objection that I've already made that statements under 92 bis are distorted statements. We've seen that through examples of witnesses from Kosovo. So they distort the picture that is being given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. None of the criteria which prevent this statement being admitted under the Rule exist, apart from those paragraphs which I've identified which would be the subject of live evidence. So the statement will be admitted subject to the live evidence on those paragraphs, 7 to 27 and 33. There will be cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pseudonyms and protection?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We've got -- let me say we've had now the observations of the amicus on this subject, so we've had a chance of reading those.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Historically, I think, there are about four features to have in mind. Looking right back to the beginning of the Kosovo phase, there was some clear over enthusiasm that had been allowed to enter into applications for protection as identified as the problem, and it's been corrected. The following three features, we've had a number of witnesses who have come here having been granted protection, and they've simply preferred to give evidence openly. The next feature --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Those -- just pausing there so we have it in mind. Those are witnesses who asked for protection, were given it, and then when they come to give evidence say that they will give evidence live. So they're in one particular category, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's then either a category or a single example of the Chamber indicating its reluctance to allow protection where a witness came with protection and having been granted in advance. The matter was reviewed, the protection was withdrawn, and indeed the witness left the Chamber altogether and returned, and gave no evidence at all. You may remember it. It's quite an extended process. The witness had come a very long way. That was, of course, something that guided us in reinforcing our own view of the desirability of open-session testimony. Then the last factor, which links with the first factor and the second point I've been making, is that the growing experience of closed-session matters being disclosed in the press has led several witnesses who may have been granted protection or who may have been minded to ask for protection to take the view that it was actually less dangerous to give evidence publicly than to give evidence with protection, confident that the protection would eventually be blown and that suspicion and identification of them would be more dangerous for them than simply to give evidence openly. And we've had one or two examples of that. One, to my personal knowledge, very recently. So that's the overall history against which the particular pseudonyms with which we are concerned may perhaps be viewed. But before I come to these two witnesses, I can perhaps just identify to remind you a little more. Very grateful to my colleagues, particularly, I think, Ms. Dicklich, for getting the material out. You'll remember that K-1 was a witness who had full protection but decided to give evidence openly once he was here. There was a witness who gave evidence without a pseudonym and was then subsequently protected on the second day. We've had one witness, C-061, who made a decision right at the end of his testimony to give up the protection that he was afforded, and we've had two witnesses, C-1 and C-034, who fall into that first category, I think, of coming here with protection and then deciding not to. Now, the position about these two witnesses is as follows, and I can give you the dates of the relevant filings: On the 17th of April, we sought protective measures pursuant to Rule 69 and 75 for delayed disclosure. It was said that the nature of their testimony and the positions they currently held exposed them to risk and, therefore, we sought delayed disclosure as to their identity. And included in those were the two witnesses, C-039, who was described as appropriately and it was said that if it were to become known that he would testify in these proceedings, he would face serious risk to his safety and other identified bodies. And then this witness, B-073, was identified in the appropriate way, said that he'd become a controversial figure, advised to leave the country by the Serb DB and, according to him, it was the accused that wanted him out of the way. In order to ensure that there is no intimidation or worse, it is requested that his identification be delayed as late as possible. Because of the political situation and the position of the Serb DB at the time, it's believed that he will be at risk. Now, this was an assessment, therefore, made of him entirely in accordance with the provisions of Rule 60 -- I'm sorry. Rule 65? 69. Thank you. I can tell you that in relation to those witnesses, the factual position was as follows: That as to General Vasiljevic, at that time and indeed throughout, he was very concerned about his identification being known ahead of the time he gave evidence and was here at the Tribunal. And as to this witness, Dragan, he wanted everything of his dealings with the OTP dealt with on an entirely confidential basis. I'll return to that a little later. But the terms of Rule 69 bear just a moment's consideration and examination because they say: "... the Prosecutor may apply ... to order the non-disclosure of the identity of a victim or witness who may be in danger or at risk until such person is brought under the protection of the Tribunal." So that was the first application. It was dealt with by the first decision of this Chamber on the 3rd of May, or by a filing of the 3rd of May of 2002 where those pseudonyms were permitted for the witnesses with whom we are concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Nice, if I understand you, in applying Rule 69, the Prosecutor does so proprio motu, not necessarily on the basis of any request from the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can go proprio motu. To some degree did in these cases, but in fact in each case each witness was expressing concerns either explicitly requiring anonymity or requiring confidentiality, which was judged the same thing, because you can't offer confidentiality without offering anonymity. And Dragan -- I'll say a little more about how he reflected his desire for anonymity later, or confidentiality. The next application was on the 30 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm reminded by the registrar that there is an initial appearance in this court at 2.15, so we really have to be out at quarter to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Very well, then, can I summarise it in this way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be we'll have to continue this tomorrow, but go on, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next application was 31st of May of last year - these are all 2002 applications, of course - where pursuant to an order of the Chamber that we should make applications for protective measures it intends to make in respect of witnesses. We made no application for protective measures at trial for either of these two witnesses. We said in paragraph 15 that witnesses will require certain protective measures relating to their testimony before the Trial Chamber, that we'd be in a better position to assess the extent of the protective measures required closer to the time when they will testify, and we requested to be permitted to file an application for trial-related protective measures for sensitive source witnesses at a time closer to the testimony, and suggested that it would be appropriate to make such applications at the time that they were disclosed to the amici. That would be 30 days before coming to testify. At that stage, General Vasiljevic was still thinking of seeking full protection. Dragan was simply somebody seeking confidentiality. An application was made for closed-session testimony for Vasiljevic, and that's dated the 17th of September, but it was rejected, so that each witness remained the beneficiary of an order for delayed disclosure and nothing more, and the pseudonym, of course, protecting the delayed disclosure. General Vasiljevic made it absolutely plain to us -- General Vasiljevic made it absolutely plain to us, for all sorts of reasons that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. require considerable explanation, that he wanted his anonymity maintained until giving evidence. He had notified us at some stage before, although it remained a little unclear until his last visit, but I think it was before that, that he would give evidence in open session. But of course with the length of time that witnesses have to wait and the changing circumstances in the territory in which they live, that wouldn't be something that could be relied on in any event because it might itself have changed back. But we had a general indication he was going to give evidence openly but he wanted protection until the moment that he gave evidence. It may be that I should have re-examined him more fully on this, but that's been our clear understanding, and thus it was in his case that he came and gave evidence in the circumstances he did. I can summarise the position for Dragan --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we've got to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. I'll come back to that tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Tomorrow morning we'll come back to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And obviously, we should hear the bit about Captain Dragan in his absence, and then the accused, if he wants to, can raise the matter with him.
